strengths: Technically solid and carefully verified: the Feynman rules are shown to reproduce the known recursion relations for the NTK tensors (A, B, D, F) from [17], with the main-text theorems backed by detailed case-by-case proofs in Appendices E-H that can be checked against prior algebraic results.

The framework appears genuinely useful as a computational tool: the new recursion relation for the 1/n correction to the NTK mean Θ{1} (Section 5.1, Appendix G) is claimed to be previously undeduced, and the all-order generalization (Theorem 4.3) plus the 1/n^2 example in Appendix F suggest the calculus scales beyond leading order.

Novel conceptual results derived with the formalism: extension of finite-width gradient-stability (criticality) results from preactivations to arbitrary NTK statistics (Theorem 5.1, with an all-order argument), and a general proof that the diagonal NTK mean is exact for all scale-invariant activations (Theorem 5.2), generalizing prior ReLU-specific results [38, 39].

Impressive numerical verification: the complete first-order recursion system (Θ{1}, K{1}, V, A, B, D, F) is implemented for arbitrary inputs and activation functions via a SymPy-based pipeline, with careful Monte-Carlo validation across widths (n ≳ 20), depths, and multiple activation functions (GeLU, ReLU, LeakyReLU, identity), including stability/instability of power-law behavior away from criticality.

Good reproducibility: implementation details, inputs, integration settings, sample sizes, and compute resources are documented in Appendices J-K; limitations (MLPs only, mostly order 1/n) are honestly discussed.
weaknesses: Incremental novelty relative to prior work: the cumulant decomposition into rank-four tensors A, B, D, F, and V, the 1/n expansion, and the preactivation Feynman rules largely exist in [16, 17, 18]. The main new element is extending the diagrammatic bookkeeping to NTK/dNTK/ddNTK lines; the recovered recursions (Appendix E) mostly reproduce results from [17], which limits the conceptual advance to a (useful) calculus rather than new physics of NTKs.

Limited demonstrated impact on ML practice: the dNTK/ddNTK tensors are defined partly to enable 1/n corrections to training dynamics and feature learning, but no actual finite-width training-dynamics predictions or feature-learning results are computed or validated; the experiments verify the recursion relations themselves rather than demonstrating downstream insights about training.

Specialized scope: results are restricted to MLPs with NTK parametrization at initialization (no biases in the stability experiments); extension to convolutions/transformers is deferred. The audience for the diagrammatic formalism is narrow, and the main text is dense for non-experts despite the claimed accessibility motivation.

The scale-invariance result (Theorem 5.2) is a modest extension of known ReLU results [38, 39], and the stability result (Theorem 5.1) is a natural generalization of the criticality bootstrap of [18]; neither carries major new practical implications.

The claimed all-order completeness (Theorem 4.3) relies on enumerating ever-growing higher-rank tensors (V6, F6, ...) whose recursions are not systematically worked out; a full higher-order analysis is explicitly left as future work, so the practical reach at O(1/n^2) and beyond remains untested beyond one example.

strengths: Technically solid formalism: the paper carefully develops Feynman rules for NTK statistics and demonstrates (Theorems 4.1–4.3, with case-by-case proofs in Appendices E–F) that the rules reproduce known layer-wise recursions from [17] and extend to higher-derivative tensors (dNTK, ddNTK) needed for training dynamics at order 1/n.

The recursion for the first-order NTK mean correction Θ{1} (Section 5.1, Appendix G) appears genuinely new, and the all-order stability result (Theorem 5.1) is a clean extension of prior preactivation-stability work [18] to the backward pass.

Extensive and convincing numerical validation: the recursions are implemented in a general, activation-function-agnostic SymPy framework, and the corrected kernels match sampled networks well at widths n ≳ 20, including convergence checks of the isolated corrections (Figures 5–10) and stability/absence-of-correction experiments across ReLU, LeakyReLU, GeLU, and linear activations.
Honest limitations section and substantial appendices with implementation details, inputs, and compute resources, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited originality: the core 1/n effective-theory framework, tensor decomposition (V, A, B, D, F), and the Feynman-diagram methodology for preactivations already exist in [16], [17], and [18]. The main novelty is extending the diagrammatic bookkeeping to NTK-type statistics — an extension that is useful but largely mechanical; the paper's own Theorems 4.1/4.2 are framed as 'recovering' existing recursions from [17].

Uncertain significance relative to the claimed motivation: the abstract and introduction motivate the work via NTK evolution and feature learning during training, yet all results are at initialization and all experiments use synthetic, hand-picked inputs. No experiment demonstrates improved prediction of actual training dynamics or feature learning, so the practical payoff for the ML community remains unproven.

Some headline results are partially known: the ReLU case of Theorem 5.2 was previously established via other approaches [38, 39], and the NNGP diagonal result is from [17]; the genuinely new content (general scale-invariant case, Θ{1} recursion) is narrow.

Restricted scope: MLPs with NTK parametrization only; no convolutions, attention, or other architectures where finite-width NTK corrections would be most impactful. The framework's generality is asserted ('no conceptual obstacle') but not demonstrated.

Presentation is dense and physics-heavy (10 rank-four tensors, colored line conventions, extensive selection rules), which limits accessibility to the ICML audience; several diagrams and equations (e.g., (7), (10), (34)) are hard to parse without color reproduction and careful cross-referencing between main text and Appendix D.

The claimed completeness at all orders (Theorem 4.3) is only argued at the level of structural uniqueness of vertices; the higher-order tensor zoo is acknowledged but not developed (beyond the D-tensor example in Appendix F), so the practical reach of the formalism at higher orders remains untested.

strengths: Technically solid framework extension: the paper develops a complete set of Feynman rules for NTK and joint preactivation-NTK statistics, which prior work ([18, 26, 28, 29, 32, 33]) restricted to preactivations only. The Theorems 4.1-4.3 are supported by explicit derivations (Appendices E.1-E.4) that reproduce the known order-1/n recursions from [17] diagrammatically, and the case-by-case verification against algebraic results is convincing.

Genuinely novel results: the recursion relation for the first-order NTK mean correction Θ{1} (Section 5.1, Eq. 12) appears to be new, Theorem 5.1 (criticality of the NNGP implies criticality of all NTK cumulants) is a nontrivial all-order result derived naturally from the diagrammatic formalism, and Theorem 5.2 generalizes the known ReLU absence-of-corrections result to all scale-invariant nonlinearities.

First numerical implementation of the full set of first-order correction recursions in the general multi-input case. The experimental validation is thorough: Fig. 1/4/5 show convergence of corrected kernels to sampled statistics from n≈20, Figs. 6-10 verify the auxiliary tensors A, B, D, F, V, and Figs. 12-25 carefully verify stability at/below/above criticality and the scale-invariance claims (ReLU, LeakyReLU vs. GeLU), with appropriate error estimates, repetition counts, and even a discussion of numerical sensitivity at large widths.

Substantial and honest limitations section: restriction to MLPs, restriction to order 1/n in practice, and acknowledgment that higher-order tensor analysis is out of scope. Compute resources are documented.

The implementation methodology (SymPy symbolic recursions, marginalization of Gaussian integrals, contraction/symmetry reductions) is described in enough detail (Appendix J) to make the numerical claims plausible and reusable.
weaknesses: Significant overlap with prior work in the core results: much of the technical content consists of reproducing recursions already derived in [17] via algebra (the text itself repeatedly notes 'agrees with the expression found in [17]'). The genuinely new results (Θ{1} recursion, Theorems 5.1/5.2) are valuable but relatively narrow. The paper is best viewed as a methodological/efficiency contribution rather than new physics about networks.

The motivating claims about training dynamics are under-delivered: the abstract and introduction emphasize NTK evolution and feature learning as key payoffs of finite-width NTK statistics, but all experiments are at initialization. No experiment demonstrates a correction to actual training dynamics or feature learning, so the practical significance for ML practitioners remains asserted rather than demonstrated.

The all-orders claim (Theorem 4.3) is argued semi-informally in Appendix E.4; the uniqueness argument for cubic vertices and the enumeration of higher-rank tensors is plausible but not a rigorous proof at the level of the order-1/n theorems.

Restricted scope of the framework in practice: MLPs only, NTK parametrization only, and the recursions require expensive numerical integration of up to 4-dimensional Gaussian expectations per layer; the paper does not analyze how the computational cost scales with depth or number of inputs.

Presentation issues: heavy reliance on appendices for essentially all proofs and definitions; the dense tensor notation (10+ named tensors) is hard to internalize; the diagrammatic notation is genuinely useful but the selection rules (Appendix D) are intricate and would benefit from worked intuitive examples. There are multiple typos and grammatical errors ('Their the definitions', 'disccused', 'dinstinct', 'has let to'). No explicit statement that code is released, which weakens reproducibility of the numerical implementation.
Theorem 5.2's novelty over [38, 39] is limited to generality of the scale-invariant class; the paper acknowledges the ReLU case was previously established.
